page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Degenerate orbitals are orbitals of the same
They differ only in the magnetic quantum
number m, that is, in their orientation.
steps.why: Scope first, because the card was not explicit about it before 2026-08-25: this marked answer is written for a multi-electron atom, which is the general case the board asks about, and every example and common mistake below is read in that scope. Orbitals of one subshell share n and l, so they share the energy as well. Only the orientation differs, and orientation costs no energy unless a magnetic or electric field is applied. The hydrogen atom is the stated exception: it has one electron, its energy depends on n alone, so in hydrogen 2s and 2p are degenerate as well. Both statements are correct in their own scope, and the exam answer uses the multi-electron one.
common_mistakes: Saying orbitals of the same shell are degenerate. In a multi-electron atom, which is the scope of this answer, 2s and 2p share n but have different energies. Hydrogen is the one exception, where they are equal.
Leaving out the words equal energy, which is the whole definition.
steps.memory_tip: Same subshell means same energy. Only the direction changes.
steps.margin_note: Name the quantum number m. It shows why the energies are equal. Write the answer for a multi-electron atom.

The five 3d orbitals are degenerate in the
steps.why: The p subshell is the smallest clear example, with three orbitals of equal energy. Hund's rule applies to exactly this set, which is why the term is defined before that rule is stated.
common_mistakes: Giving 2s and 2p as the example. In a multi-electron atom their energies are not equal, so that pair does not show degeneracy.
Giving only the name of a subshell without saying how many orbitals it holds.
steps.memory_tip: Three p orbitals, five d orbitals. Each set is degenerate within itself.
steps.margin_note: Writing n and l for the example proves the energies match.
